evidence_quotes.quote: This analysis sampled end-use consumption data from 97 of 1630 geographically stratified households from 14 enumeration zones in two adjacent villages.

Our analysis effectively disaggregates daily per capita demand for socio-demographic attributes, including income level, household size, length of tenure, different water access typologies and wastewater sinks.

We apply RWEUA to explore how diverse consumption practices and behaviours, socio-demographic attributes, and household infrastructures distribute demand for water and wastewater services in a single model.

Typically, households with a tenure of greater than 30 years demonstrated lower overall water demand (100.0 lpcd), as well as for toilet flushing, bathing, dishwashing, and clothes washing (see Fig. 7).
Overall, households that access water primarily via a reticulated supply (12.3 %, 150.8 lpcd) or header tank (39.2 %, 116.4 lpcd) demonstrate higher than average indoor water demand.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household water supply access typologies (public and private reticulated piped water, private boreholes to header tanks or storage vessels, hand pumps, rainwater, and purchased bottled water), sanitation containment/disposal configurations (septic tanks, pit latrines, sewer connections, faecal sludge collection), and residential end-use water demand in two villages in Siem Reap Municipality, Cambodia.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, the study does not examine any legal, administrative, regulatory, or governance rule-type mechanism governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, tenure/documentation requirements for connection, tariff or cost-recovery rules, discretion, enforcement, or utility regulatory structure). Under the plain/literal wording of Criterion 2, the study also fails because its empirical determinants are socio-demographic attributes (village location, income level, household size, and duration of residence termed 'length of tenure'), household fixtures/appliances, and water-use behaviours in a microcomponent residential water end-use balance model. Decentralisation, master planning, and urban vs. peri-urban zoning (Wat Svay vs. Kakranh) serve only as unanalysed background context motivating demand-forecasting methods; 'ID Poor' status is used solely as a survey proxy to classify low-income households; and 'length of tenure' (Section 3.2.4) measures years of residence (<10, 10-20, 20-30, >=30 years) reflecting cultural/vernacular housing cohorts rather than legal tenure rules or documentation requirements (owner vs. tenant status is reported only descriptively in Table 1 and never analysed as a determinant of access).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical data from a geographically stratified random sample of 97 households (534 residents) across 14 census enumeration zones in two villages, using a semi-structured survey questionnaire, structured observation protocol, and empirical flow-rate and storage measurements.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports household water consumption quantity in litres per capita per day (lpcd) across indoor and outdoor end-uses, alongside prevalence of household water access typologies and wastewater/sanitation containment and disposal methods.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (97 households and 534 residents in Wat Svay and Kakranh villages, Siem Reap Municipality), study exposures/determinants (water access typology, household fixtures/practices, village of residence, income level, household size, and years of residence), outcomes (per capita and per household daily water end-use volumes and wastewater sink flows), and study design (cross-sectional stratified household survey and residential water end-use water-balance analysis) are clearly reported.

study_design: Cross-sectional stratified random household survey, structured observation, empirical flow measurement, and bottom-up residential water end-use balance modelling
population_and_sample: 97 randomly stratified households (534 residents) out of 1,630 households across 14 census enumeration zones in two adjacent villages (Wat Svay, n = 57; Kakranh, n = 40) in Siem Reap Municipality, Cambodia
exposure: Water access typology, household fixtures/appliances and water-use practices, village location (Wat Svay vs. Kakranh), household income level, household size, and duration of residence ('length of tenure' in years)
outcome: Residential end-use water demand (frequency, duration, flow rate, and volume in litres per capita per day and litres per household per day) across indoor/outdoor microcomponents and distribution across water supply typologies and wastewater sinks
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). While the paper empirically measures household water access typologies, sanitation containment/disposal sinks, and daily per capita water consumption across 97 households in Siem Reap, Cambodia, it is a socio-technical residential water end-use analysis (RWEUA) designed to generate bottom-up microcomponent water-demand parameters for infrastructure planning. It does not examine any legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor—neither under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading nor under the plain wording of Criterion 2. Specifically, 'length of tenure' in the analysis measures duration of residence in years (reflecting post-conflict and migration cohorts and vernacular housing styles) rather than legal land tenure or documentation rules, 'ID Poor' status is used solely to classify household income, and municipal decentralisation/planning frameworks are unanalysed background context.
